1:
"And Joshua the son of Nun sent out of Shittim two men to spy secretly, saying, Go view the land, even Jericho." Gill and Wesley both press the tense before anything else: the verb is better read had sent, the errand belonging to the days before the order to break camp. Gill places Shittim in the plains of Moab, the Abelshittim that Josephus calls Abila, sixty furlongs and better from Jordan, and reports the Jewish tradition that the two were Caleb and Phinehas — which he rejects, since neither was a young man and men of that rank would hardly be spent on such an errand. Meaner persons, he judges, but men of good sense and ability, and of probity: two good men, in Kimchi's phrase, and not as they that went on the mission of Moses.

That earlier mission governs how the witnesses read this one. Henry remembers that Joshua had himself been one of the twelve, and that it proved of ill consequence; so this time the survey is of Jericho only and the report comes to Joshua only, not to the whole congregation. Calvin draws the distinction more sharply still. The twelve were sent to make a thorough survey of the land and to be heralds of its excellence, stirring up the courage of the people; these two are sent to ascertain whether a free passage may be had over the Jordan, and whether the citizens of Jericho are indulging in security or are alert and prepared to resist. He notices the awkwardness the accounts make together — that the people asked for the first mission and that Moses elsewhere says he sent them by command of God — and raises a question he does not dismiss: are we to approve Joshua's prudence, or condemn him for an excessive anxiety that trusted his own foresight without consulting God?

Henry answers it in the other direction, and makes the answer a rule. Faith in the promise ought not to supersede our diligence in the use of proper means but to encourage it; Joshua is sure he has God with him, and yet sends men before him. We do not trust God, but tempt him, if our expectations slacken our endeavours. Wesley reads the secrecy the same way, and notes where it points: not at the enemy, which is the practice of all spies, but at Israel, lest a discouraging report get abroad before Joshua had weighed it.

The lodging is given without comment or apology. Wesley observes that the Hebrew word is used elsewhere in the same sense and is so rendered by two apostles, and that Rahab either now was such or rather had been formerly; that they lodged there is simply that they lay down. Then the city wakes. Gill supposes watchmen set to observe what passed, or citizens acting for their own safety; Calvin thinks it would have argued extreme supineness to let unknown strangers pass freely through a frontier town with Israel encamped near and the Red Sea crossing already noised abroad. Keil and Delitzsch carry the report to its consequence: the king, suspecting why they had come, sent to Rahab to give them up. Clarke finds the summons itself revealing — had she been a woman of ill fame he could have seized them as vagabonds, but a guest under a householder's roof was sacred through all the east, and had to be demanded.
4:
"And the woman took the two men, and hid them, and said thus, There came men unto me, but I wist not whence they were." Gill and Wesley again read the verb as a pluperfect: she had taken them, before the king's messengers arrived, on a rumour already abroad that she had Israelite spies under her roof. Wesley makes the timing the measure of the act — she understood from her neighbours that the thing was suspected, guessed that search would be made, and acted; and he counts this the great and generous act of faith for which she is afterwards praised, since she plainly ventured her life on a steadfast persuasion that God's word to Israel was true.

The concealment fixes the season, and three witnesses say so independently. Calvin observes that had the time of year not been known from elsewhere, the stalks of flax would have settled it: the crop is taken from the ground at maturity and laid in the open air to dry before the woody fibre is stripped from it, and flax sown about the end of September is pulled at the end of March or the beginning of April — which is precisely when Israel began to move camp. Clarke reaches the same date and adds that the Hebrew word for the stalks carries the sense of wood, so that hemp or flax, it was in its rough unmanufactured state, freshly pulled and drying on the roof; and he recalls that eastern houses are flat-roofed by law and custom, walked on, talked on, and often slept on. Ellicott notes only that flax and barley are both early crops and that the first month was the time of barley harvest.

Then comes the lie, and here the witnesses divide. Calvin frames two questions and refuses to hurry either: was treachery to her own country excusable, and could the falsehood be free from fault? The love of one's country is implanted in us by nature, and Rahab knew the object was the overthrow of the city where she had been born and bred. Clarke will allow her nothing on the second count — the darkness was friendly to the whole plot, and in daylight the spies could scarcely have escaped, but this is no excuse for the woman's prevarication, since God could have saved his messengers independently of her falsity, and never says to any, Do evil that good may come of it. Wesley agrees the answer was false and therefore unquestionably sinful, though her intention in it was good, and suggests that as a heathen she might well have thought an officious lie no crime at all. Ellicott puts the same thing as a distinction rather than a verdict: the falsehood evidently left no stain on her conscience, although all falsehood is sin, for the divine standard of sin and holiness never varies while the standard of a man's conscience, even where faith is the dominant principle, may vary considerably.

The pursuit empties the city and shuts her in with her guests. Wesley glosses the fords as the places where people used to pass over Jordan, and notes that the gate was shut behind the pursuers in case Rahab had been mistaken and the men were lurking still. Calvin reads the credulity of the pursuers as a blinding, and the closed gate as a fresh trial: the city was now a prison, the hope of escape cut off, and the two were awake and in alarm when she came to them. What strikes him is that she was not dismayed at all, but bargained for her own life and her family's with entire composure — which is where he finds the lively faith that the apostles saw in her.
8:
"And she said unto the men, I know that the LORD hath given you the land, and that your terror is fallen upon us." Keil and Delitzsch set the scene closely: the officers gone, she came up to the roof before the two had lain down — they were probably about to sleep there, as men did in the East — and confessed to them everything she believed and knew. He marks the pronouns. The us on whom the terror has fallen is not Jericho only but the Canaanites at large, set over against the you of Israel; and the words in which she describes their despair are the words of the song Moses and the people had sung at the sea, so that what was then sung as hope is here reported as accomplished fact by one of the nations it was sung against.

Henry reads the speech as the whole reason the mission was worth making: not merely that the late victories over the Amorites in the neighbouring country were known, but that the deliverance out of Egypt and the passage through the sea — a great way off, and forty years ago — were remembered and talked of afresh in Jericho, to the amazement of everybody. Gill fastens on the same interval, that they had heard and remembered it though it was forty years since.

Calvin weighs the two reports against each other and finds them of unequal force. The opening of the sea was a full and irrefragable proof, as much so as if God had stretched forth his hand from heaven, since water would never have changed its nature and stood in heaps unless the author of nature had so ordered it; the victories over the kings east of Jordan were a testimony too, but one resting on inference. Between them they seized all minds with the conviction that God himself was the principal leader of the expedition — though Calvin suspects the Canaanites drew the wrong conclusion, imagining the God of Israel had merely proved stronger than the gods of Egypt.

What she says next goes past anything that reasoning would supply. Clarke calls the confession amazingly full, arguing considerable light: she owns him omnipotent and omnipresent, and in consequence hid the spies and risked her own life. He then asks how she came by such knowledge, and offers three answers without choosing between them — that some knowledge of the true God was general in the earth at that time, though tangled with the superstition that gave each district and people its own deity, one god for the mountains and another for the valleys; that she had it from the spies, with whom she appears to have had a good deal of conversation; or that it came by a supernatural influence upon her own soul. What he will say is that she made better use of her light than her countrymen did, and that God increased it.

Calvin sees her faith in the sentence as in a mirror. Casting down all idols, she ascribes the government of heaven and earth to the God of Israel alone, and that is a repudiation of the whole pagan arrangement by which majesty and power are portioned out among many. She speaks in absolute terms: whatever power exists resides in him, and he orders things above and below. Yet Calvin will not overstate it. Her faith was not fully developed; it was a germ of piety, as yet insufficient of itself, and he says so plainly while insisting that in surrendering herself to that power she gave proof of her election. Keil and Delitzsch judge it the same way, that her confession fell short of what Moses was at that moment demanding of Israel. Wesley needs one line for the effect of it all on her neighbours: melted, that is, dissolved, having lost all courage.
12:
"Now therefore, I pray you, swear unto me by the LORD, since I have shewed you kindness, that ye will also shew kindness unto my father's house, and give me a true token." Gill notes that she asks for a religious action, binding on men that feared the Lord, and that the Targum has her say swear to me by the Word of the Lord. Clarke takes the form of the request as further proof that she had been instructed: she acknowledges the true God by his essential name, and knows an oath sworn in it to be the deepest obligation a man of Israel could come under. Wesley adds that swearing by his name is one eminent act of his worship.

Calvin finds the deepest evidence of her faith not in the oath but in what she assumes before asking for it. She places the sons of Abraham in sure possession of the land on no ground but that she has heard it was promised them; she does not suppose God is favouring lawless intruders forcing their way into other men's territories, but concludes they come because he has assigned them the dominion of it. The promise was no secret — those nations knew what had been said to Abraham. So in her language Calvin hears what the apostle means by calling faith a sight of things that do not appear: she sits in a fortified city, and commits her life to two terrified fugitives.

Keil and Delitzsch define the token she asks for. It is literally a sign of truth, by which they should guarantee the kindness requested; and it consisted in nothing but the solemn oath itself, sworn in the words our soul shall die for you. The list she wants covered is exact. Gill observes that no husband and no children are named, as with such women they seldom are, and reports Abarbinel's remark that father and mother stand in the room of a husband, brothers and sisters in the room of children. Wesley says the same more briefly, that for herself it was needless to speak, since saving their preserver was a plain and undeniable duty; and he cannot leave the verse without noting how far the sequel outran the request — this is all she asks, but God did for her more than she could ask or think, and she was afterwards a princess in Israel, the wife of Salmon, and among the ancestors of Christ.

Ellicott lingers on the family list. Whatever Rahab herself may have been, her acknowledgment of all her kindred is observable: she was in no way separated or degraded from their society. Setting the chapter beside what Moses says elsewhere of Canaanite practice, he concludes that she was morally not inferior to her countrymen but rather their superior — and remembers that publicans and harlots were not the worst members of the evil and adulterous generation to whom the Word came, but believed the Baptist and were among the most constant hearers of the true Joshua.

The spies answer with their own lives. Clarke glosses it as the old practice of pledging, staking a man's life for his neighbour's. Calvin will not soften the form of words: they imprecate death upon themselves, constituting themselves a kind of expiatory victims if any evil should befall Rahab through their negligence, and the pledge covers her parents and her brothers and sisters too. Therein, he says, lies the sanctity of an oath — that though its violation may escape with impunity so far as men are concerned, God has been interposed as witness and will take account of the perfidy. Wesley admires the one condition they attach, that she not divulge the business: in managing the oath with so much circumspection they showed piety and prudence together, ensnaring neither their own consciences nor the public justice.
15:
"Then she let them down by a cord through the window: for her house was upon the town wall, and she dwelt upon the wall." The situation of the house is what makes the escape possible. Clarke explains that either the city wall formed part of it or it stood hard against the wall, so that its upper storey rose above with a window looking to open country; the gates being shut, there was no other way out. Wesley adds that her own dwelling was up there, the rest of the house perhaps kept for the entertainment of strangers. Ellicott thinks the spies may have chosen the place for that reason, since it let them leave without passing the gate. Gill pictures the mechanics — the window large, the cord strong — doubts she trusted any servant with the secret, recalls that Paul was let down the wall of Damascus in a basket, and reports Jarchi's grim suggestion that it was the same cord and window by which her visitors had come and gone. Clarke notes the verse stands out of its place, since she cannot have let them down before the terms of the following verses were settled; Wesley reads the whole conversation as having passed inside, since they would hardly discuss such weighty matters hanging on a rope.

Her advice is local knowledge. Gill identifies the mountain as the one now called Quarantania, and borrows a traveller's account of the prospect from it over the land of the Amorites, of Gilead and of Bashan, and of the neighbouring Adummim through which the road from Jerusalem to Jericho is cut — the road, he observes, where the man fell among thieves. Ellicott makes the same connection drily, that those mountains have often sheltered worse characters than Joshua's spies. Clarke supposes they travelled by night; Wesley reckons the three days one whole day and parts of two.

Then the spies fence their oath about. Keil and Delitzsch count three conditions, on the failure of any of which they stand released. The first is the token in the window, and here the witnesses divide over what the token was. Keil takes "this cord" to be the rope of the previous verse, since no other object has been mentioned for the demonstrative to point to, and Luther concluded the same; Wesley likewise thinks it the same she was about to let them down by. Ellicott rejects that flatly: the scarlet line and the lowering cord are different words in the original, and it would have been preposterous to require her to hang out the means of escape, declaring the whole tale to every beholder — the very thing she had sworn not to do. He connects the line instead with the flax already on her roof, so that what hung at the window would look unremarkable while telling those in the secret which house to spare. Clarke calls it simply a piece of scarlet cloth hung out by way of flag.
19:
The second condition draws a line at her doorstep. Keil and Delitzsch give it in its legal form: whoever went out of the doors into the street bore his blood upon his own head, so that if he were slain outside by Israelite soldiers he carried his death as his own fault, while whoever stayed with her in the house was upon the spies' head if any hand were laid on him. The formula, Keil observes, is the standing legal one, the same construction by which the law elsewhere lays a man's blood upon himself. Wesley puts it plainly: the blame would rest wholly on the man himself, by his own neglect of the means of safety, while for those inside the spies declared themselves willing to bear the sin and shame and punishment of it.

Ellicott hears another night behind the arrangement. The words are close to the charge given in Egypt — that none of them should go out at the door of his house until the morning, while the Lord passed through to smite — and he draws the comparison out: what the blood on the lintel and the two side-posts was to the houses of Israel in Egypt, the scarlet line in the window was to the house of Rahab, the one prefiguring what the other prefigured.

The third condition is her silence, and Clarke thinks it prudently framed. It was wise to make her life depend on her secrecy; otherwise she might have been tempted to give information not only about the spies but about the designs of Israel, whereas with her own safety and her relatives' staked upon it she had every motive to keep the secret. Gill sees a particular mischief guarded against: were the business uttered, others might either hang out scarlet threads of their own or crowd into her house for shelter, and the token would protect whom it was never meant to protect.

She agrees to everything. Gill notes the exactness of her assent — that if the conditions were not performed they should be quit of their oath, but that if they were, she expected it to be kept. Then she sent them away and bound the scarlet line in the window. Keil and Delitzsch are careful about the timing of that last clause: she can hardly have tied it there at once, but only when it was needed, and the writer mentions it at this point simply to bring the subject to a close. Wesley takes the other view and thinks she did it forthwith, partly so that the spies might see it hung out before their departure and know it again at a distance, and partly lest some accident should occasion a neglect about it later.
22:
"And they went, and came unto the mountain, and abode there three days, until the pursuers were returned." Keil and Delitzsch identify the range: the hills on the northern side of Jericho, afterwards called Quarantana, a wall of rock rising almost sheer from the plain to twelve or fifteen hundred feet and pitted with grottoes and caves along its eastern face. They were well adapted for hiding, and they were the nearest high ground to the city, the western range receding considerably to the south. Gill names the same mountain, and Wesley adds the detail that made three days possible at all — they were living on the provisions Rahab had furnished. He also marks where the search went: along the road to Jordan and the places near it, but not into the hills.

The reckoning of the days interests three of the witnesses separately. Clarke counts them out — concealed that night, all the next day and the following night, and returning on the third. Gill reports Kimchi's calculation that the descent fell on the third day from their being sent, which was the second of the three days Joshua had spoken of. Ellicott states the principle rather than the arithmetic, that it probably means the completion of three days from the beginning of the mission, by the usual inclusive reckoning of the Old Testament.

Henry makes the safe return itself the first half of the good news. Had these two been disposed to discourage the people, as the spies Moses sent had been, they had ample material: the height and strength of the walls of Jericho, the vigilance of its king, and how narrowly they had escaped out of his hands. But they were of another spirit, and depending on the promise themselves they animated Joshua too. That God had provided them so good a friend as Rahab in an enemy's country, and brought them back in peace through all the rage of the king and the eagerness of the pursuers, was in itself a token for good: he who so wonderfully protected the scouts would preserve the men of war and cover their heads in the day of battle.

The report they bring is the exact reverse of the earlier one. Clarke sets the two side by side — how different from what was brought on that former occasion — and notes that the inhabitants were panic-struck, having heard what was done to the kings of the Amorites and concluding that nothing could stand before Israel; which was precisely the information Joshua needed for laying his plan of campaign. Calvin reads the same words as a testimonial to the men themselves. Their language proves them right-hearted and of rare integrity, he says; others, not yet recovered from the terror they had been thrown into, would have disturbed the whole camp, whereas these reflect on the kindness that brought them out and exhort Joshua and the people to go boldly forward. And though the bare promise of the land ought to have sufficed, God is so indulgent to their weakness that he confirms by experience what he had already spoken — the spies arguing, as Rahab had argued before them, from the fainting of the inhabitants to the certainty of the gift.

Clarke will not close the chapter without going back to the lie, and he answers plainly. Did Rahab lie to the king's officers? She certainly did; and the inspired writer sets the fact down as it stood, without making the Spirit of God responsible for the woman's dissimulation. Was she not rewarded? She was — for her hospitality and her faith, not for her falsehood. Could she have saved the spies without it? She certainly might.
